body:
Source: issue #5
https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/issues/5

The branch now contains the four corrective implementations summarized in the updated PR body. Local validation passed: make check, make architecture-check, make linux-compat-check, three kernel-policy unit tests, and the complete make test QEMU boot.

Final corrective update is pushed at `d1539711`. The branch now includes the implementation fixes, QEMU 10/11 VT-d compatibility, a hardened packet-timeout self-test, and x86-hosted QEMU CI.

Verification:
- Local `cargo test --package ginux-kernel-policy`: 4 passed
- Local direct kernel clippy: passed
- Local `make test`: `GINUX_KERNEL_OK` and `Boot test passed.`
- Final GitHub Actions run: static passed in 2m22s; full QEMU boot passed in 6m29s

CI: https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/actions/runs/41180277867

No merge or close action was taken.

This is an adversarial review generated by Grok Bot (an AI assistant) at Vince's request, checked against the code at `d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f`. Findings may contain mistakes; please verify.

**Summary.** This PR does real work: a focused `linux_random.rs` extraction, warning-denying kernel clippy, read-only CI that actually boots the kernel, a corrected compatibility ledger, and a reconciliation doc. Several claims go further than the code, though:
- **`make test`:** the "passes" claim only holds for the QEMU that Homebrew ships today. On QEMU 10.0.13 it still fails (#4).
- **QEMU suite stability:** once that is patched around, the suite is flaky on an x86-64 host, in the same native-volume recovery invariants that the runner switch was meant to avoid.
- **Unsafe ratchet:** it doesn't enforce its own acceptance criterion.
- **Gate-14 doc:** it marks items "Resolved" that are resolved by a global kernel-entry lock (or, for the paper, not changed).

None of this argues against merging the CI and lint pieces. It argues against ticking #5's boxes on the strength of this PR's wording.

**What I ran** (x86-64 Linux VM, 8 vCPUs, Rust 1.99.0 via `rust-toolchain.toml`, clang/lld 19, Debian QEMU 10.0.13 + OVMF 2025.02, TCG because the VM has no KVM access):
- **`make check`:** passed (architecture checks, unsafe baseline `1033 / 109 / 1`, compat `53/257/48/17/0`, kernel clippy, `ginux-kernel-policy` 4 tests).
- **`make test` on this head:** fails with `ginux: virtio network initialization invariant failed` (#4).
- **`make test` on this head + #10:** the kernel reaches `GINUX_KERNEL_OK`, then `boot.sh` fails on its hardcoded `queue size: 256` grep.
- **`make test` on this head + #10 + a local 2-line `boot.sh` fix:** I ran it 12 times and it **passed 3**. Six were default runs (2 passed), three used `QEMU_TCG_THREAD=single` (1 passed), and three used `GINUX_CPUS=1` (0 passed). All 9 failures were native-volume invariant panics, with 5 distinct messages: `post-descriptor-rejection recovery`, `post-ABI-rejection recovery`, `replacement native volume service`, `post-fault native volume recovery` and `post-cancellation native volume`.
- **Unsafe ratchet bypass:** a scratch edit adding an `unsafe fn` (raw pointer write) and an `unsafe impl Sync` passed `check-kernel-unsafe.sh` unchanged.

Severity: **P0** critical correctness/security bug or a false claim, **P1** high (claim overstated in a way that matters, or the property isn't actually enforced), **P2** medium, **P3** low, **P4** minor, **P5** nit. "Overengineering risk" estimates how likely a fix is to grow into new machinery that isn't needed yet, and says what not to build.

### Findings

- [ ] **P1: the QEMU suite is flaky on an x86-64 host too, so the runner switch hid the problem rather than fixing it**
  - Evidence: [`17-ci-kernel-policy-tests.md#L65-L73`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/hdae/gates-todo/17-ci-kernel-policy-tests.md#L65-L73) says run `41179498965` "failed a separate native volume recovery invariant under x86 QEMU cross-emulated on the macOS arm64 runner", and that the job now uses `macos-15-intel` "so the x86-64 guest is not cross-architecture translated". But `default_accelerator` only picks KVM on Linux ([`common.sh#L52-L58`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/tools/qemu/common.sh#L52-L58)), so the Intel macOS runner also uses TCG, which binary-translates either way. On an x86-64 host I hit the same class of failure in 9 of 12 runs (see "What I ran"), including with one guest CPU and with single-threaded TCG. So it isn't an arm64-host or MTTCG artifact. (My VM is shared and may have been under load, but so are CI runners, and that is the point.) The CI green is 2 runs on the new runner ([`41179779273`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/actions/runs/41179779273), [`41180277867`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/actions/runs/41180277867)). It's worth noting the paper's own host is Apple Silicon ([`BENCHMARKING.md#L66`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/BENCHMARKING.md#L66)), which is exactly where this failed in CI. This PR doesn't touch the native-volume code, so the flakiness is probably pre-existing. But this is the PR that claims `make test` passes and turns it into CI.
  - Smallest fix: open one tracking issue with a failing log, and reword the gate evidence to "intermittent on TCG; under investigation". Then look at what those recovery invariants wait on. Every failure I saw is a post-fault/post-rejection recovery check, which smells like a deadline or poll budget that TCG speed can miss.
  - Overengineering risk: **Medium.** Don't build a retry/quarantine harness, a multi-runner matrix, or a deterministic-replay setup. One issue, a loop of ~10 local runs and, if it's a timeout, one budget change is the proportionate response.

- [ ] **P1: `make test` still fails on QEMU 10.0.13, so "`make test` passes / delivery gap corrected" depends on the Homebrew QEMU version**
  - Evidence: on this head, the boot panics at [`lib.rs#L931-L941`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/lib.rs#L931-L941). That's the `== 256` assertion from #4, which #10 fixes in the kernel. Even with #10, [`boot.sh#L170-L171`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/tests/qemu/boot.sh#L170-L171) greps for `queue size: 256`. The workflow installs whatever `brew install qemu` gives ([`check.yml#L25`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/.github/workflows/check.yml#L25)), and that already broke once on QEMU 11's VT-d encoding.
  - Smallest fix: land #10 plus the two `boot.sh` greps (accept any power of two ≥ 8, and allow the trailing `\r`), and print `qemu-system-x86_64 --version` in the CI log.
  - Overengineering risk: **Low.** Don't add a QEMU version matrix. One version log line and the #4 fix are enough for now.

- [ ] **P1: the unsafe ratchet doesn't enforce "new unsafe blocks fail checks"**
  - Evidence: [`check-kernel-unsafe.sh#L7-L22`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/tools/architecture/check-kernel-unsafe.sh#L7-L22) counts the text `unsafe {` and the text `SAFETY:` across the whole tree. Because of that:
    - **`unsafe fn` and `unsafe impl` aren't counted.** That's 61 and 25 today. Under edition 2021 an `unsafe fn` body is an implicit unsafe block. A scratch edit adding `pub(crate) unsafe fn f(a: u64, v: u64) { *(a as *mut u64) = v; }` plus an `unsafe impl Sync` passed unchanged.
    - **Swaps pass.** Removing one block anywhere and adding an undocumented one elsewhere passes. So does adding any `SAFETY:` comment anywhere.
    - **This PR does it itself.** The new [`linux_random.rs#L13-L64`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu/linux_random.rs#L13-L64) has 3 `unsafe` blocks and an `unsafe impl Sync` with 0 `SAFETY:` comments, and it passes.

    This contradicts the acceptance criterion at [`16-kernel-unsafe-lint-enforcement.md#L39`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/hdae/gates-todo/16-kernel-unsafe-lint-enforcement.md#L39). The kernel clippy run doesn't cover this either, because `clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks` is allow-by-default.
  - Smallest fix: keep the count as a coarse ceiling, and in new or extracted modules (starting with `linux_random.rs`) add `#![deny(clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks, unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn)]` and write the four missing `SAFETY:` comments. Optionally count `unsafe fn|impl` in the script, which is a one-regex change. Reword the criterion to "the total doesn't grow" if that's what's intended.
  - Overengineering risk: **High.** It would be easy to respond with a custom unsafe inventory tool, an AST-based checker, or a push to document all 1,033 blocks. None of that is needed now. Per-module clippy lints on code you touch, ratcheting outward, achieve the property with zero new tooling.

- [ ] **P1: `sendmmsg` (307) and `recvmmsg` (299) are still `Complete` after `sendmsg`/`recvmsg` became `Partial`**
  - Evidence: [`LINUX-COMPATIBILITY.md#L761`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/LINUX-COMPATIBILITY.md#L761) and [`#L769`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/LINUX-COMPATIBILITY.md#L769). Both loop over the now-`Partial` paths ([`cpu.rs#L28472`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L28472), [`#L28552`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L28552)). They also return `EINVAL` for `vlen > 64` where Linux clamps to 1024, and `recvmmsg` writes a zero timeout back instead of the remaining time ([`#L28612`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L28612)). The Gate-14 table says this ledger item is "Corrected" ([`GATE-14…md#L25`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/feedback-hardening/GATE-14-CRITICISM-RECONCILIATION.md#L25)). (This is the same finding as in my #11 review; the files are identical.)
  - Smallest fix: mark both `Partial` and update the totals to 51/259.
  - Overengineering risk: **Low.** It's a label change. Socket semantics work is separate.

- [ ] **P2: `rdrand` inline asm is declared `preserves_flags` but writes CF/OF/SF/ZF/AF/PF**
  - Evidence: [`linux_random.rs#L13-L20`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu/linux_random.rs#L13-L20) runs `rdrand` then `setc` with `options(nostack, preserves_flags)`. `RDRAND` sets CF and clears the other status flags, so the option is a false promise to the compiler, which is undefined behavior under Rust's inline-asm rules. It's latent today, but an optimizer change could keep a comparison result in flags across this block. This is moved code, not new, and it's the only `rdrand`/`rdseed` use in the kernel.
  - Smallest fix: drop `preserves_flags` (keep `nostack`), and add a `// SAFETY:` line while you're there.
  - Overengineering risk: **Low.** It's a one-word fix. Don't turn it into an audit of every `asm!` block.

- [ ] **P2: the Gate-14 table says "Resolved" for globals and exclusion, which is true only because of one global kernel-entry lock**
  - Evidence:
    - **Globals and exclusion:** [`GATE-14…md#L20-L21`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/feedback-hardening/GATE-14-CRITICISM-RECONCILIATION.md#L20-L21) mark "globals cannot survive SMP" and "exclusion relies on one CPU" as Resolved. State still lives in 213 `Banked*` statics in `cpu.rs`, and syscalls are serialized by a single `KERNEL_ENTRY_LOCK` ([`sync.rs#L32`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/sync.rs#L32), [`#L180-L182`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/sync.rs#L180-L182), taken at [`linux_syscall.rs#L11`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu/linux_syscall.rs#L11) and [`#L59`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu/linux_syscall.rs#L59)). A big kernel lock is a legitimate design for this stage, but the table should say that's the mechanism.
    - **Paper item:** marked "Resolved in repository reporting" ([`#L26`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/feedback-hardening/GATE-14-CRITICISM-RECONCILIATION.md#L26)), but this PR doesn't change the paper. The "Observed ratio 3.31×" column is still there ([`ginux-ai-systems-report.tex#L591-L593`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/paper/ginux-ai-systems-report.tex#L591-L593)). The existing caveats are real, so "Won't change; caveat retained" would be accurate, but "Resolved" isn't.
  - Smallest fix: reword the three rows, for example "Mitigated: correct under SMP via a global kernel-entry lock; state not yet per-process/per-thread" and "Not changed; existing caveat retained".
  - Overengineering risk: **High.** Don't respond by starting fine-grained locking or migrating `Banked*` state into process objects just to earn the word "Resolved". The BKL is fine for now. Fix the wording.

- [ ] **P2: the doc's own "Maintainer response" section contradicts its table**
  - Evidence: [`GATE-14…md#L55-L60`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/feedback-hardening/GATE-14-CRITICISM-RECONCILIATION.md#L55-L60) still says "CI and kernel unit-test coverage are still missing, and the compatibility ledger's Complete labels remain internally inconsistent", while rows [`#L24-L25`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/feedback-hardening/GATE-14-CRITICISM-RECONCILIATION.md#L24-L25) say "Corrected". It's stale text from the reconciliation-only first round.
  - Smallest fix: update or delete that paragraph.
  - Overengineering risk: **Low.**

- [ ] **P3: "the kernel has no unit tests" is marked Corrected, but the kernel crate still has 0 `#[test]`s**
  - Evidence: [`GATE-14…md#L24`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/docs/feedback-hardening/GATE-14-CRITICISM-RECONCILIATION.md#L24). The new crate ([`kernel-policy/src/lib.rs`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/crates/kernel-policy/src/lib.rs)) holds four validators (about 40 lines) with 4 tests. The PR description says "3 passed", but `cargo test` shows 4. That's a good seam, and Gate 17 itself is careful ("Do not claim that host tests replace QEMU"). The row is the part that overstates.
  - Smallest fix: say "Started: host-tested `kernel-policy` seam (4 validators)". If you want one more function, pick something with arithmetic edge cases, such as the iov/mmsg bounds or the virtio queue validator from #10.
  - Overengineering risk: **High.** Don't build a hosted-kernel test harness, HAL mocks, or a plan to make `cpu.rs` host-testable. The QEMU suite is the real kernel test. Grow the seam one pure function at a time, only when it pays.

- [ ] **P3: the QEMU CI job sits on a deprecated runner with an unpinned emulator**
  - Evidence: [`check.yml#L22-L25`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/.github/workflows/check.yml#L22-L25). GitHub says `macos-15-intel` is the last x86-64 macOS image, available until about August 2027 ([actions/runner-images#13045](https://github.com/actions/runner-images/issues/13045)), and Homebrew has announced Intel macOS drops to Tier 3 from September 2026. Ubuntu runners have `/dev/kvm`, and `default_accelerator` would pick KVM there, which is faster and closer to the "same x86-64 KVM host" the benchmarking doc asks for.
  - Smallest fix: try the QEMU job on `ubuntu-24.04` with the usual `/dev/kvm` udev rule and distro QEMU. If that's not viable, keep the job and log versions.
  - Overengineering risk: **Low.** Don't build self-hosted runners or a runner matrix for this.

- [ ] **P4: the packet-wait helper's "full second" depends on TSC frequency**
  - Evidence: [`packet-wait.S#L267-L269`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/packet-wait.S#L267-L269) changes `100000000` to `1000000000` TSC ticks with a comment saying "a full second of guest TSC time". That's a second only at 1 GHz. Making the window 10× wider is a reasonable fix for a 10 ms deadline test, but the comment overstates the precision.
  - Smallest fix: reword the comment to "10^9 TSC ticks (≈0.3–1 s)".
  - Overengineering risk: **Low.** Don't add TSC calibration for a test helper.

- [ ] **P4: committed `generated_boot.rs` doesn't regenerate identically on another host**
  - Evidence: this PR updates [`generated_boot.rs`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/boot/efi/src/generated_boot.rs), a signed, embedded blob. After `make check`/`make test` on my host with the pinned Rust toolchain, the file differs from the committed one (about 14.9k lines). I didn't investigate why (clang version, paths, or ordering). It means a CI check like `git diff --exit-code` would fail today, and that blob changes in PRs can't be reviewed by regenerating them.
  - Smallest fix: none required for this PR. Note it as a known limitation.
  - Overengineering risk: **High.** Fully reproducible builds is a project of its own. Defer it.

### Claims checked and confirmed
- `linux_random.rs` is a faithful move: the random, boot-ID and getrandom logic is unchanged. Only visibility widened to `pub(crate)`, including the `LinuxBootIdCell` `UnsafeCell` field, which is worth narrowing back to `pub(super)`. The backing statics stay in `cpu.rs` for the runtime-owner inventory. `cpu.rs` is 42,752 lines, as stated.
- The kernel now calls the `ginux-kernel-policy` validators ([`cpu.rs#L41457-L41465`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L41457-L41465), [`iommu.rs#L306`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/d1539711c179930214ee8443663a7ba01017215f/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/iommu.rs#L306)), and the 4 host tests pass.
- The VT-d fault check is still strict after accepting both no-PASID encodings: the valid bit is required, read transactions and reserved bits (including PASID-present) are rejected, and reason = 5 and source must match.
- Kernel clippy with `-D warnings` runs in `make check` and passes. The toolchain is pinned (`1.99.0`), so new clippy releases won't break CI unexpectedly.
- The workflow has read-only `contents` permission and runs `make check` and `make test`. Both CI jobs passed on the head commit.
- `GINUX_BOOT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` is validated as a positive integer.
- The 17 `Unsupported` reclassifications and the 12 socket `Partial`s are correct (see my #11 review).
- Gate 14 correctly keeps the private entry-path report out of the public record.
